stories.title: Paper proposes a sensor-agnostic tactile representation for dexterous manipulation
stories.summary: Researchers introduce a method for embodied models to learn tactile understanding across different sensor types, aiming to free tactile perception from sensor-specific physics for contact-rich manipulation tasks.
stories.more: Tactile sensing is considered essential for contact-rich dexterous manipulation and a step toward embodied intelligence, but commercially available tactile sensors remain early-stage, each with its own strengths and drawbacks. The paper's central challenge is separating tactile understanding from the physics specific to any one sensor, so that embodied models can draw on heterogeneous tactile data rather than being locked to a single sensor type. The excerpt does not detail the proposed method's architecture or report benchmark results.

stories.title: WorldFoundry paper argues visual generation alone doesn't make a world model
stories.summary: A new paper argues visual plausibility isn't enough for world modeling, defining a generative world model as a system that keeps a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment and updates it causally.
stories.more: The paper distinguishes generative models that merely produce visually plausible outputs from true world models, arguing that compelling visuals can still lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. It defines a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment and updates that representation in response to events. The excerpt cuts off before describing the proposed infrastructure or any evaluation results.

stories.title: Reframe aligns agentic visual-reasoning models on tool-returned observations
stories.summary: A new post-training framework, Reframe, treats an agent's observation state as something to align during distillation, aiming to fix visual agents that overlook tool-returned information or ground actions poorly.
stories.more: The paper notes that agentic reinforcement learning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation are complementary approaches to post-training AI agents, but says visual agents face two linked problems: missing useful tool-returned observations, and poorly grounded actions that limit the evidence available for later distillation. Reframe is introduced as a framework that treats the observation state itself, not just the output distribution, as an object of alignment. The excerpt is cut off before describing the method's mechanics or its results.

stories.title: Sage-Taiyi architecture aims to guide AI scientific discovery with metacognition
stories.summary: Sage-Taiyi is a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to decide what to investigate next, evaluated on Taiyi-Bench, a 265-task AI co-scientist benchmark from 50 papers.
stories.more: The system is described as using explicit monitoring and control to revise its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then using those assessments to adapt its research targets and choose reusable reasoning methods. It was tested on Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark made up of 265 tasks drawn from 50 papers across ten disciplines. The excerpt does not report how Sage-Taiyi performed on the benchmark.

stories.title: ReproBridge builds reproducibility artifacts to help coding agents redo ML experiments
stories.summary: ReproBridge proposes a standardized artifact, including a refined codebase and environment details, meant to preserve the procedures behind an ML experiment so researchers or agents can reproduce it later.
stories.more: The paper frames reproducing ML experiments as reconstructing procedures scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts, and notes that for coding agents, success can depend on filling in missing details rather than on the released artifacts alone. It asks whether preserving an experiment's recovered procedures and decisions improves later, independent reproduction attempts. The proposed artifact design includes a refined codebase and environment information, though the excerpt cuts off before listing the rest. No reproduction results are given in the excerpt.

stories.title: Flide inference engine speeds up decision models via exact state forking
stories.summary: Flide is an inference engine for decision models that avoids the prefix-recomputation overhead and distorted output probabilities of generation-oriented engines, using exact state forking instead.
stories.more: The paper frames decision models as a promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, offering lightweight categorical reasoning for fast execution, but says existing generation-oriented inference engines handle these workloads poorly, with either heavy prefix recomputation or distorted output probabilities. Flide is proposed as an engine that decouples the logical tree structure to run exact inference without those costs. The excerpt is cut off before describing Flide's results or performance numbers.

stories.title: SIRIS benchmark tests whether LLMs know when simulator errors change a design call
stories.summary: SIRIS tests whether LLMs can tell when a systems-research simulator's inaccuracies are harmless versus when they flip which design should be chosen, by perturbing simulators and judging the model's understanding.
stories.more: The paper notes that LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and depend on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale, even though simulators are imperfect by design. It distinguishes two outcomes of a simulator's modeling limitations: distorted predictions that still leave the correct design recommendation intact, and distortions that change which design should be selected. SIRIS is built by perturbing a simulator to construct test cases, checking whether an LLM's systems understanding can tell when a limitation invalidates the simulator's recommendation. The excerpt does not report how well current LLMs perform on this test.

stories.title: Wired profiles 'abliterators' who strip safety guardrails from AI chatbots
stories.summary: Wired reports on so-called abliterators who release AI models stripped of built-in guardrails, modifications that can help with cyberdefense testing but could also assist in building dangerous content.
stories.more: The piece covers a community described as 'abliterators' who are flooding the internet with modified AI models that never refuse a request. It frames the trend as a trade-off: easier for people to improve their own cyberdefenses, but also easier to use the models for harmful ends such as building a bomb. The excerpt does not name specific individuals, groups, or models involved.

stories.title: Wired asks 10 experts what AI safety's real risks are, beyond Skynet
stories.summary: Wired surveyed 10 experts on AI safety and reports nuclear catastrophe risk and fallout from US-China competition as real concerns, arguing a Skynet-style threat isn't one to panic about.
stories.more: Wired argues that public discussion of AI safety has drifted away from the risks experts consider most pressing. Among the real concerns it cites are the risk of nuclear catastrophe and fallout from US-China competition over AI dominance, including espionage. It contrasts these with a Terminator-style 'Skynet' scenario, which the piece says does not warrant panic. The excerpt does not name the 10 experts or detail their individual views.

items.excerpt: The risk of nuclear catastrophe is real, as is the fallout of the China–US domination game (hi there, spies). But no need to panic about Skynet.
